issues.issue: "The present contract" is not identified by date or title, and the only contract booklet elsewhere referenced is the expired 1981-84 booklet (paragraph 14), so what body of terms the six-year "Contract" consists of is left open. The reader cannot tell from these words whether side letters and memoranda are part of the "present contract" or only preserved separately by paragraph 14.

The "additional $3.67 per shift from wages and after taxes ... shall be contributed to the Welfare Fund" does not say whose money it is — an employer contribution or an employee wage deduction remitted to the Fund — nor whether it is owed for shifts beyond the five-shift maximum. That characterization determines the size of the employer's contribution obligation.

The same $3.67 is described in the Section 13-H.1 amendment (Appendix, "add 'and an after tax deduction from wages of $3.67'") as a deduction from wages rather than as a contribution to the Welfare Fund, and the two descriptions cannot both be given literal effect. A court asked how much is owed to the Fund would have to reconcile paragraph 2(a) with that amendment.

Paragraph 2(a) expressly directs that "Pension and welfare contributions shall be made on this amount" for the 1987 increase, while paragraph 2(b) states the 1989-1992 increases with no such direction, inviting a negative-implication argument that contributions are not owed on them. The relationship between the two subparagraphs, not the figures, is what would be construed.

The clause fixes no formula, base period or multiplier for the cost-of-living adjustment, deferring wholly to unspecified "relevant provisions of the Contract," and the bracketed Index sentence does not say whether the measurement runs May-to-May or January-to-January. The 1992 Memorandum's later stipulation that adjustments "utilize a January to January rather than a May to May Index" shows the gap.

The opening sentence is incomplete — "shall have full force and effect at the Edison, New Jersey [gap] by The Times within the Northeast Corridor" — so the class of facilities covered (Edison only, or every new or rebuilt plant in the Corridor) cannot be read off the words. The later garbled passage about listing protected regular situation holders leaves the same scope question open.

"Any issues under this paragraph" has no fixed referent: the mediation sentence sits in a separate block from numbered paragraph 3, so it is unclear whether mediation reaches only new/rebuilt-facility arbitrations or all disputes under paragraph 3. The command that "the arbitrator shall issue his award before operations commence" is also stated as mandatory yet immediately assumes he may not.

The me-too right is keyed to "any labor organization" followed by a parenthetical list of nine named unions, leaving it open whether the list is exhaustive (expressio unius) or merely illustrative. "Wage and benefit package" is likewise undefined as against the productivity/attrition and diversion provisos.

The obligation is to execute such documents "as are necessary to administer" the Welfare Fund, an open-ended standard with an illustrative "including but not limited to" list, so what The Times must actually sign is undetermined. Whether that reaches the Fund's trust agreement and its delinquency machinery is left to argument.

As with 5(a), the duty to execute documents "as are necessary to administer" the Pension Fund states no standard for necessity and no limit on the documents covered. The Fund's own trust agreement (Article 9) purports to govern rate, mode and enforcement of contributions, so what 5(b) commits The Times to is uncertain.

The disclaimer that nothing requires The Times "to expend any funds beyond its obligation to make contributions" is hard to square with the Fund trust agreement's Article 9.4, which imposes interest, liquidated damages and collection costs on a delinquent employer. A delinquency defendant would invoke 5(c) as capping its exposure at contributions alone.

"Various shop disputes" is not identified, and the provision's whole content depends on Appendix A, whose heading in the executed document is garbled. Which disputes were resolved, and whether anything outside Appendix A survives, cannot be told from the text.

The nondiscrimination ground list — color, race, sex, religion, national origin — is closed, with no catch-all, so age, disability and other protected characteristics are excluded by negative implication. "Any other condition of employment" is also undefined against the specific reference to hiring.

The paragraph recites that Section 3-H.2 coverage is being raised "from $60,000," but Section 3-H.2 of the 1981-84 Collective Bargaining Agreement states $20,000, and $50,000 beginning January 1, 1982. The premise of the increase cannot be squared with the section it amends, leaving the covered class and prior amount in doubt.

"Group I employees not so scheduled" has no antecedent anywhere in this Memorandum — the scheduling premise lives only in Section 13-J of the Collective Bargaining Agreement — so the class covered by the new jury-pay formula is unstated. It is also unclear whether the eight-week look-back replaces or supplements the existing differential pay.

"Plants" is capitalized but undefined, and the revision changes Section 6-D from "more than one plant" to "one or more Plants," so whether a staging facility, annex or the 43rd Street building counts as a plant is open. The disjunctive "foreman or assistant foreman" also leaves the required rank indeterminate.

The letter is said to be "attached as Appendix C," but the executed document labels its attachments only "Appendix A" and "Appendix B," and the weekly-contribution letter carries no Appendix C designation. Which writing paragraph 11 incorporates has to be worked out from the instrument as a whole.

The Section 3-P letter is said to be "attached as Appendix D," yet no attachment in the executed document bears that label, the 3-P letter appearing between two blocks marked "Appendix B." The cross-reference cannot be matched to the papers actually annexed.

Paragraph 13 refers to a letter of understanding "attached as Appendix E," but the only arbitrator-related letter in the document (the neutrals-designation letter) is marked Appendix B and fixes no designations. What the parties agreed to execute cannot be identified from the attachments.

Paragraph 14 preserves "all letter agreements, side agreements ... in effect on the date hereof," which cannot be squared with Appendix A's abolition of the November 22, 1983 West Side Direct Routes Memorandum and with the September 9, 1988 letter saying that abolition leaves the rest of that memorandum intact. Which instrument controls the West Side Direct routes turns on reading the three together.

Paragraph 15 contemplates a later-executed "New York Times Agreement" embodying the modified Contract, while paragraph 1 says the Contract simply is the present contract as changed by this Memorandum; if the new document was never executed or departs from the Memorandum, the two provisions point to different governing texts. Paragraph 14's supremacy sentence does not say which prevails over a subsequently executed consolidated document.

Effectiveness "immediately following Union ratification" is hard to square with paragraph 1's term running from March 31, 1987 and paragraph 2's increases and Welfare Fund contributions made "effective March 31, 1987" in a document signed in August 1988. Which obligations run from ratification and which retroactively is left to construction.

The chapeau condition — "subject to there being no increase in the number of floor hires as set forth in the Collective Bargaining Agreement" — sits awkwardly against the creation of ten additional floor regular situations, and neither the baseline number nor the consequence of an increase is stated. Whether the condition is a precondition or a limitation on staffing is unresolved.

The five additional dayside chauffeurs are not said to be regular situations, unlike the floor positions in the same sentence, and "(4 days and Monday night)" does not state the shift pattern for each. Their status under the chapeau's floor-hire condition is therefore unclear.

The provision requires an update "to reflect the names of the two employees that presently hold these job bids" without naming them or attaching the revised pages 104-5. The content of the amendment is not ascertainable from the writing.

Delivery is to "delivery points designated by the Publisher," an unbounded unilateral discretion with no standard limiting relocation or number of points. "Shall continue to be served" also fixes no baseline practice against which continuation is measured.

This paragraph abolishes the November 22, 1983 West Side Direct Routes Memorandum outright, while the September 9, 1988 Bishow letter ("West Side Directs") says the abolition affects only the attrition portion and leaves every other agreement about those routes intact. The two cannot both be given full effect.

The cross-reference is to "Appendix B-1," but the document contains an "Appendix B" side letter on Honor Boxes and Vending Machines and no Appendix B-1. What is incorporated must be inferred from the instrument as a whole.

"Any existing physical pick-up of such copies shall continue" leaves "such copies" ambiguous between all returns and only the excepted unsold bulldog copies, which are the copies most immediately referred to. The scope of the preserved pick-up practice turns on that antecedent.

The commitment to "maintain present Practices" in honor box and vending machine deliveries defines neither the practices nor the date at which they are frozen, and "The Times direct operation" is broader than the West Side Direct area later described. What must be maintained is left entirely to extrinsic proof.

Weekly Welfare Fund payment cannot be squared with Section 13-H.1 of the 1981-84 Collective Bargaining Agreement, which requires payments "on the basis of weekly employment" to be made "at least once a month, unless the Trustees of the Fund determine that more frequent payments are necessary." Whether the letter supersedes that provision, and for whom, is a live question in any delinquency claim.

"Made available" no later than ten days after the payroll week is not the same as paid or received, so the date on which a contribution becomes delinquent is undefined. The letter is also undated ("July , 1988"), leaving the ratification-plus-30-days trigger to be fixed by extrinsic evidence.

"The Grandfather or Grandmother of a Regular Situation Holder or Group I Extra or of his or her spouse at the time the grandparent dies" is syntactically ambiguous: the closing phrase may qualify the spousal relationship, the employment status, or merely fix the date of the event. The letter also does not say whether step- or in-law grandparents count, which is the very inconsistency it was written to cure.

The cut-off is "a death occurring prior to the date hereof," but the letter bears no date at all ("July , 1988"), so the retroactivity line has no fixed reference point. Whether the operative date is the letter, ratification, or execution of the Memorandum is unresolved.

The replacement first sentence of Section 13-K.2 is unreadable in the executed document ("may elect to accumulate a ll ef hi ... unused"), so the new accumulation right cannot be ascertained from the words. The accompanying deletion of the fifth sentence also breaks off mid-quotation, leaving it unclear how much is deleted.

"Certain neutrals" are neither named nor made identifiable, and the letter fixes no consequence or default mechanism if the parties meet within sixty days and fail to agree on designations. What the parties are actually bound to do is left open.

The obligation is only "to negotiate the conditions" for a run, with no obligation to establish it and no standard for the negotiation. "When the normal daily order reaches 2500 copies" also leaves "normal daily order" undefined — over what period, and whether Sunday counts.

The trigger for the Monday Lancaster assignment depends on the parties having "agreed upon satisfactory arrangements" and on a "revised Glen Burnie agreement" being "put into effect," none of which is defined or dated, so the thirty-day clock may never start. The proviso that the delivery "shall not involve The Times in increased costs" sets no baseline for measuring cost.

The duty to negotiate is conditioned on the parties having "resolved satisfactorily any grievances, differences and disputes" about Edison work and staffing — an open-ended condition with no objective test or deadline. "Additional portions" of the Magazine and the no-increased-cost proviso are likewise unquantified.

The amendment says the change to "7.678%" merely reflects "the present welfare contribution percentage," yet Section 13-H.1 as written states 6-1/2%, and no effective date is given for the new rate. When the 7.678% obligation began, and on what base it is computed, is not stated.

The 7.678% figure does not match the 7.68% health and welfare contribution rate recited in paragraph 8 of the 1992 Memorandum of Agreement, which also caps total plan contributions at 15.68%. Which percentage governs contributions in the overlapping period must be resolved between the two documents.

The insertion is a quotation that is never closed — add "and an after tax deduction from wages of $3.67 after the words "per shift" — so it cannot be told whether the inserted words end at "$3.67" or include the locating phrase, or which occurrence of "per shift" is meant. The amended text of Section 13-H.1 is therefore indeterminate.

This subparagraph calls the $3.67 an "after tax deduction from wages," while paragraph 2(a) of the Memorandum says the same $3.67 per shift "shall be contributed to the Welfare Fund." Whether the Fund is owed that amount as an employer contribution cannot be answered from either provision alone.

The first-year figure is illegible in the executed document ("3/31/87 = §.00 per shift"), so the additional contribution for the initial contract year cannot be determined from the writing. The schedule also does not say whether the five-shift weekly cap in Section 13-H.1 applies to these amounts.

"Casuals" is a term Section 13-H.1 never uses; that section identifies the class by exclusion — employees who are not regular situation holders, Group 1 or Group 2 extras, or Group 3 extras working more than 180 days. Which employees the increased per-shift contributions cover requires reconciling the two texts.

The amendment operates by inserting words "after the words 'notify the Union' in the last sentence" of Section 9B without reproducing that sentence, and closes with "[balance as in original]," so the amended provision cannot be read from this text. Which sentence is the "last sentence" of Section 9B is itself unstated.

"This shall only apply to a New York Times part or section regularly inserted in the Sunday or daily newspaper" leaves "This" ambiguous between the new sixty-day written notice and the whole of Section 9B, and "regularly inserted" is undefined. The escape clause — no notice required if The Times "can demonstrate that it did not have sixty (60) days' notice itself" — supplies no standard of proof or of "promptest practicable notice."

"A uniform portion of each employee's wage increase" sets no cap, no method of election, and no definition of uniformity across classifications. Whether the diversion applies only to the March 31, 1990 increase or to every later increase ("to become effective then or thereafter") is likewise open.

"Nominal administrative costs" fixes no ceiling, so the sole limit on the diversion's cost to The Times has no measurable boundary. "Any such alternatives" also refers to alternatives never enumerated in the letter.

The parties agree only to "study possible methods" through a four-member committee, with no deadline, no decision rule for a tie, and no obligation to implement anything. Whether the paragraph creates any enforceable duty at all is nameable.

The object of the guarantee is missing from the executed text — "it will guarantee all Saturday night Bulldog [gap] uding routes and relays)" — so what is guaranteed (routes, jobs, a number) cannot be read off the words. The condition "so long as it has a Saturday night Bulldog Edition" also leaves the guarantee terminable at The Times' election to drop the edition.

"The gross wages paid such employees in 1987" has no antecedent — the paragraph is the first in the letter and never identifies the employee group covered by the Earnings Bonus. "Notwithstanding any provision to the contrary" likewise identifies no provision it overrides.

The same annual 3.86% rate is applied to a three-month period without saying whether the figure is prorated or applied whole to that period's wages. The 1993 stub period also has no separate W-2, which paragraph 4(a) makes the measure of "gross wages."

"Gross wages" is tied to the W-2 Form "for the applicable bonus period," but paragraph 3 creates a bonus period of January 1 to March 30, 1993, for which no W-2 exists — W-2s report a calendar year. The definition and paragraph 3 cannot both be applied literally.

The addition is triggered by shifts for which the employee receives benefits "under The Times Disability Plan," yet the amounts added are state disability and workers' compensation benefits, which need not correspond to those shifts. The "to the extent" carve-out for amounts appearing on the W-2 also leaves partial overlaps unresolved.

The general sixty-day payment deadline cannot be squared with paragraph 6, which requires the January 1 to March 30, 1993 bonus to be paid "within thirty (30) days after March 30, 1993," nor with paragraph 7's sixty days from termination. Which deadline governs a given bonus period is a question of reading the paragraphs together.

The fallback directs that $25.93 be "allocated in the manner set forth in Paragraph 7," but Paragraph 7 sets out a Union termination right during the contract term and no allocation manner for a post-March 30, 1993 cessation. The cross-reference cannot be given effect as written.

The trailing phrase "in connection with the current extension negotiations or at any time through March 30, 1993" is syntactically adrift — it may qualify the fringe benefits negotiated by another union, or the Union's window for exercising the termination right. The scope of the right the Union reserved turns on which reading is taken.

The paragraph deems wage scales increased by $25.93 for any benefit "calculated on or determined by the employee's wage rate," expressly including "Times retirement or pension benefits," and then excludes contributions to the Publishers'-NMDU Welfare Fund and the NMDU-Publishers' Pension Fund; the inclusion and the carve-out pull against each other. Which pension and welfare items fall on which side of the line is the whole question.

The carve-out sits against Section 13-H.1 of the Collective Bargaining Agreement, which fixes the Welfare Fund contribution as a percentage of "each employee's rate per shift," so whether the deemed increased rate feeds that percentage cannot be answered from either text alone. A Fund seeking contributions computed on the higher deemed rate would have to be met by reading the two together.

"The number in the first sentence of Paragraph 3 is now eighty-eight (88)" does not say what the number counts, and the referenced Memorandum of Understanding at pp. 103-5 of the 1981-84 contract book (as changed in January 1984) is not reproduced. The amendment has no ascertainable meaning on its face.

The letter asserts that the enclosed Spinelli memorandum states "the practices continued by the side letter agreement," but the Appendix B side letter preserves present practices for Honor Boxes and Vending Machines throughout "The Times direct operation," while the memorandum describes only vending machines in the West Side Direct area. The two cannot be equated without narrowing or expanding one of them.

The list of the three drop locations is scrambled and incomplete in the document, so the second and third locations cannot be identified with confidence. It is also unstated whether the recited figures (three locations, 121 machines) fix a practice or merely describe one at a moment in time.

This letter says the "abolition" of the November 22, 1983 Memorandum affects only "that portion providing for attrition of those routes," whereas Appendix A of the Memorandum of Agreement abolishes that Memorandum entirely and gives The Times the right to reorganize the West Side Direct routes. Which of the two controls the surviving route obligations cannot be answered from either alone.
